analysis.one_liner: Extends family leave and equal-treatment protections to part-time and temporary workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it sits without action.
analysis.plain_summary: Most protections under the Family and Medical Leave Act — unpaid, job-protected leave for a serious illness or a new child — only apply to workers who have been on the job 12 months and worked at least 1,250 hours in the past year, which screens out most part-time workers. This bill would replace that test with a simple 90-day employment requirement, so part-timers could take the same protected leave. It would also make it illegal to pay part-time, temporary, or short-duration workers less than full-time workers doing substantially the same job, or to give them worse schedules, benefits, or promotion chances, and it would require employers to offer available hours to current employees before hiring new ones — and to pay current employees when new hires take hours they wanted.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans who work part-time, temporarily, or on short schedules. They would gain access to protected family and medical leave after 90 days on the job, a legal right to equal pay and benefits for equal work, and a claim on available hours before any new hire gets them.

how_it_helps.text: The FMLA currently requires 12 months on the job and 1,250 hours in the prior year before a worker can take protected family or medical leave; the bill replaces that with a 90-day employment requirement, opening leave to part-timers.

It makes it illegal to pay part-time or temporary workers less, or give them weaker schedules, benefits accrual, or promotion access, for jobs that involve substantially the same skill, effort, and duties as full-time workers' jobs.

Employers must record each worker's desired weekly hours at hire and must offer existing employees those hours before hiring anyone new — and must pay an existing worker for each hour a new hire works during the existing worker's stated available time if the worker wasn't scheduled for their desired hours.
Workers can sue for back pay, doubled liquidated damages, and reinstatement, and the Labor Secretary can investigate, fine, and sue on workers' behalf.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in retail, food service, and other industries that rely heavily on part-time and temporary staffing. They would face higher wage and benefit costs for equal work, new scheduling and recordkeeping duties, and potential lawsuits and fines — and could no longer fill hours cheaply with new hires while existing part-timers want more hours.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face new administrative burdens: documenting every worker's desired hours, checking those statements before hiring externally, and paying existing workers for hours performed by new hires during their stated availability — a requirement with unusual reporting and payroll implications.

The bill counts employees across franchise networks and integrated enterprises toward the 15-employee threshold, which some franchisors argue effectively imposes obligations on small individual franchise locations.

The equal-treatment rule limits legitimate pay distinctions tied to seniority and merit but still invites litigation over whether differences were truly hours-based, and employers would bear the burden of defending routine pay decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to part-time workers — many of whom are women, caregivers, and low-wage hourly employees — would be substantial: family leave access and equal pay and scheduling treatment for work they already do. The costs fall on employers in scheduling, recordkeeping, and pay; the pay-for-unfilled-hours requirement is the most demanding provision, and critics would argue it creates real administrative burden and could make employers cautious about part-time hiring. Those costs do not, however, change the direction of the bill's benefits, which run squarely to workers rather than to any concentrated interest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and no further action has been taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 17, 2025 and read twice.
It was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it has remained with no markup, vote, or floor action.
No version of the bill has received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that depend on lower pay and benefits for part-time staff are better off so far, since the bill has not advanced and would raise their labor costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers relying on cheap part-time labor

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Booker, Markey, Padilla, Whitehouse, Sanders, Murray, and Baldwin

sides.party_line_note: All eight Senate sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Republican supports the bill, and it sits in a committee chaired by the majority.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurants, and other large hourly-work employers
industries.note: These industries rely on part-time and variable-hour staffing with lower pay and thinner benefits than full-time roles; the bill would require equal pay and benefits for equal work and priority scheduling of existing staff, cutting into that labor-cost advantage.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and temporary labor firms
industries.note: Employers could no longer bring in temp or contract workers to fill hours that existing part-time employees have said they want, shrinking a market these firms currently serve.

The bill counts employees across a whole franchise network toward the 15-employee coverage threshold, so small franchise locations would be covered via their franchisor's aggregate size — a structural change to how franchise labor is regulated.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has only Democratic and independent support and no Republican cosponsors in a Senate where the majority is Republican; with 7 sponsors and no committee action since referral, it is very unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote this Congress, which is the usual fate of a minority-party labor bill introduced late in a session.
